And it is the entire reason the company is interesting. [...] AI infrastructure has turned into a physical supply-chain story, and the market keeps working its way down it: GPU, switch, optics, laser, wafer, epitaxy, and finally the tools that grow the epitaxial layers. Aixtron is in that last layer. The thesis in one line: AI needs more optical connectivity, that needs more lasers, lasers need more epitaxy, epitaxy needs more tools, and Aixtron sells the tools. The honest finding, stated up front, is that the market has largely identified this layer as well. What survives the work is one asymmetric name and a short watch list, and the discipline of saying so is the point of the piece. [...] One distinction has to come first. Two separate production flows feed an AI accelerator, and they are routinely conflated. The first is the HBM stack itself: thinning each DRAM die, forming the vertical interconnects, bonding the dies, and filling the gaps. The second is the package substrate that carries the logic die and the HBM stacks together. The stack flow is driven directly by HBM die volume. The substrate flow is driven by accelerator package count and complexity, where HBM is one input among several. Suppliers in the first flow have cleaner exposure to HBM unit growth. Suppliers in the second are exposed to AI accelerator demand more broadly. Keeping the two apart prevents the common error of treating every name here as a direct proxy for HBM. [...] The substrate node builds the FC-BGA package everything sits on, where the binding constraint is yield, not throughput. Two separate production flows feed an AI accelerator, and they are routinely conflated. The first is the HBM stack itself: thinning each DRAM die, forming the vertical interconnects, bonding the dies, and filling the gaps. The substrate flow is driven by accelerator package count and complexity, where HBM is one input among several. Suppliers in the first flow have cleaner exposure to HBM unit growth. Modern desktop processors contain up to 2,000 copper traces running through their carrier; server-grade AI chips have many times more. As AI accelerators have grown more complex, the ABF layer count has risen from 4–6 layers for a standard PC chip to 8–16 layers for an AI accelerator, and top-tier GPUs like Nvidia’s Blackwell and Rubin architectures push that to 15–18 layers. What survives the work is one asymmetric name and a short watch list, and the discipline of saying so is the point of the piece. [...] One distinction has to come first. Two separate production flows feed an AI accelerator, and they are routinely conflated. The first is the HBM stack itself: thinning each DRAM die, forming the vertical interconnects, bonding the dies, and filling the gaps. The second is the package substrate that carries the logic die and the HBM stacks together. The stack flow is driven directly by HBM die volume. The substrate flow is driven by accelerator package count and complexity, where HBM is one input among several. Suppliers in the first flow have cleaner exposure to HBM unit growth. Suppliers in the second are exposed to AI accelerator demand more broadly. Keeping the two apart prevents the common error of treating every name here as a direct proxy for HBM. snippet: Part 2 left readers with a covered and priced set of names. The three HBM producers are in structural undersupply through 2027; the market knows it, and their shares reflect it. Part 3 goes one layer down, into the sub-$50 billion suppliers whose revenue depends on HBM and advanced packaging but whose analyst coverage is thin. The honest finding, stated up front, is that the market has largely identified this layer as well. What survives the work is one asymmetric name and a short watch list, and the discipline of saying so is the point of the piece. [...] One distinction has to come first. Two separate production flows feed an AI accelerator, and they are routinely conflated. The first is the HBM stack itself: thinning each DRAM die, forming the vertical interconnects, bonding the dies, and filling the gaps. The second is the package substrate that carries the logic die and the HBM stacks together. The stack flow is driven directly by HBM die volume. The substrate flow is driven by accelerator package count and complexity, where HBM is one input among several. Suppliers in the first flow have cleaner exposure to HBM unit growth. Suppliers in the second are exposed to AI accelerator demand more broadly. Keeping the two apart prevents the common error of treating every name here as a direct proxy for HBM. [...] The substrate node builds the FC-BGA package everything sits on, where the binding constraint is yield, not throughput. Two chokepoints sit beneath the makers: Ajinomoto holds over 95% of the insulating film, and MEC Company holds over 90% of the surface chemistry that bonds copper to it. Both capture value regardless of which substrate maker wins a socket, and Ajinomoto is not investable as a chip play. Among the makers, Ibiden and Unimicron dominate and sit well...TRUNCATED...

When Barber asked “That’s Aixtron, for example?”, the answer was yes, with a caveat I come back to later. I ran the conversation through NotebookLM and had it map the chain: [...] Aixtron is not an AI company in any way you would recognize from a headline. It does not sell accelerators, run data centers, assemble modules like Fabrinet, or sell lasers like Lumentum and Coherent. It sells the equipment used to manufacture compound semiconductors. And it is the entire reason the company is interesting. [...] AI infrastructure has turned into a physical supply-chain story, and the market keeps working its way down it: GPU, switch, optics, laser, wafer, epitaxy, and finally the tools that grow the epitaxial layers. The current shock raises the specter of spillovers to the U.S. through both prices and physical shortages of goods. A critical conduit for spillovers through these channels is via Asian supply chains, especially from middle- to lower-middle income countries in southeast Asia, which are key suppliers for goods needed for the AI infrastructure build-out in the U.S. These countries are also heavily reliant on Middle East energy imports. The index had been gradually climbing even before the conflict began, likely in part reflecting strains from the boom in artificial intelligence investment. Within the GSCPI model, the increases in the index have been driven predominantly by lengthening delivery times and growing order backlogs. The SEC data JSON format is fully documented and freely available for every US public company, but the shape surprises most developers the first time they open it. This post walks through the structure of the SEC XBRL JSON endpoints, how to filter facts by form and period, and what a minimal parsing pipeline looks like in Python. [...] This is Apple' [...] A single company will have hundreds of tags under`us-gaap`, plus a small`dei`(Document and Entity Information) block with metadata like`EntityCommonStockSharesOutstanding`. One useful property of the Company Facts endpoint: it exposes only standardized taxonomies (`us-gaap` and`dei`), not the company-specific extension tags that also exist in the raw XBRL instance document. What survives the work is one asymmetric name and a short watch list, and the discipline of saying so is the point of the piece. [...] One distinction has to come first. Two separate production flows feed an AI accelerator, and they are routinely conflated. The first is the HBM stack itself: thinning each DRAM die, forming the vertical interconnects, bonding the dies, and filling the gaps. The second is the package substrate that carries the logic die and the HBM stacks together. The stack flow is driven directly by HBM die volume. The substrate flow is driven by accelerator package count and complexity, where HBM is one input among several. Suppliers in the first flow have cleaner exposure to HBM unit growth. Suppliers in the second are exposed to AI accelerator demand more broadly. Keeping the two apart prevents the common error of treating every name here as a direct proxy for HBM. snippet: Bottom Line. Mega-cap AI earnings confirm that AI has moved from pilot-cycle experimentation to production-scale deployment, but the cleaner framing is capacity-rationed demand rather than simple revenue acceleration. Alphabet, Amazon, Microsoft, and Meta all showed visible AI usage, backlog, and monetization, while also disclosing higher capex, component inflation, and rising dependence on custom silicon. The highest-conviction long exposure remains the bottleneck stack across accelerators, ASICs, CPUs, HBM and DRAM, networking, power, cooling, and data-center deployment. The key debate is whether backlog converts into attractive cash returns after memory inflation, depreciation, energy cost, direct hardware sales, and GPU substitution from Trainium, TPUs, Maia, Cobalt, and Meta-Broadcom silicon. The platform winners are those with identity, data, distribution, security, commerce, and usage-based monetization; the pressure points are PC demand, open-web traffic, agency labor, legacy IT, point SaaS, and hyperscaler free cash flow optics. [...] The demand signal is now visible in three forms: backlog, usage intensity, and direct product monetization. Alphabet disclosed $462 billion of Cloud backlog, Amazon disclosed $364 billion of AWS backlog excluding a recently announced Anthropic commitment above $100 billion, and Microsoft disclosed $627 billion of commercial RPO including OpenAI. Two separate production flows feed an AI accelerator, and they are routinely conflated. The first is the HBM stack itself: thinning each DRAM die, forming the vertical interconnects, bonding the dies, and filling the gaps. The substrate flow is driven by accelerator package count and complexity, where HBM is one input among several. Suppliers in the first flow have cleaner exposure to HBM unit growth. Two separate production flows feed an AI accelerator, and they are routinely conflated. The first is the HBM stack itself: thinning each DRAM die, forming the vertical interconnects, bonding the dies, and filling the gaps. The substrate flow is driven by accelerator package count and complexity, where HBM is one input among several. Suppliers in the first flow have cleaner exposure to HBM unit growth. Two separate production flows feed an AI accelerator, and they are routinely conflated. The first is the HBM stack itself: thinning each DRAM die, forming the vertical interconnects, bonding the dies, and filling the gaps. The second is the package substrate that carries the logic die and the HBM stacks together. The stack flow is driven directly by HBM die volume. The substrate flow is driven by accelerator package count and complexity, where HBM is one input among several. Suppliers in the first flow have cleaner exposure to HBM unit growth. Suppliers in the second are exposed to AI accelerator demand more broadly. Keeping the two apart prevents the common error of treating every name here as a direct proxy for HBM. What survives the work is one asymmetric name and a short watch list, and the discipline of saying so is the point of the piece. [...] One distinction has to come first. Two separate production flows feed an AI accelerator, and they are routinely conflated. The first is the HBM stack itself: thinning each DRAM die, forming the vertical interconnects, bonding the dies, and filling the gaps. The second is the package substrate that carries the logic die and the HBM stacks together. The stack flow is driven directly by HBM die volume. The substrate flow is driven by accelerator package count and complexity, where HBM is one input among several. Suppliers in the first flow have cleaner exposure to HBM unit growth. snippet: This report introduces and applies a single high-alpha investment heuristic: identify bottlenecks in the AI supply chain, distinguish the causers (constrained suppliers whose scarcity defines the bottleneck) from the solvers (rare vendors capable of resolving it), and invest in the solvers — companies that benefit from simultaneous volume growth, pricing power, operating leverage, and multiple re-rating. [...] In Wave 1 (2023–2024), bottlenecks migrated sequentially — from NVDA’s GPU supply to TSMC’s CoWoS packaging to HBM (where SK Hynix held near-exclusive allocation) to physical data center power and cooling. Wave 1 was defined less by clear causer/solver pairs than by a chain of scarcity that rewarded whoever sat at the constraint. Companies like NVDA, TSMC, and Vertiv all extracted extraordinary pricing power from their positions within the bottleneck. Vertiv’s case was especially instructive: starting at 12x earnings with low-single-digit growth, AI-driven ASP increases flowed through a fixed cost base to drive ~2.5x FCF growth, compounded by a P/E re-rating to 25–30x — the four-factor compounding the heuristic predicts — yet this was bottleneck beneficiary economics, not bottleneck resolution. [...] center construction, electrical transformers, gas turbines, and raw materials. [...] The heuristic is simple.
